dq-visual-0006.question_text:
A $15\text{ g}$ metal ball bearing on a string is swung around a pole in a circle of radius $0.8\text{ m}$. The plane of the circular path is horizontal. The angular velocity of the motion is $4\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. What is the magnitude of the centripetal force required to maintain the motion of the ball?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.7]
\draw[thick] (0,0)--(2.4,1.5);\draw[thick] (2.4,0.3)--(2.4,2.5);\draw[dashed] (0,0)--(2.4,0.8)--(4.8,0.8);\draw[dashed] (0,0)--(2.4,0.2)--(4.8,0.2);\fill (0,0) circle (2.5pt);\node[left] at (0,0) {$15\text{ g}$};\node[below] at (3.6,0.8) {$0.8\text{ m}$};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses an incorrect conversion or omits the squared angular velocity.
Uses an incorrect radius or angular-speed calculation.
Does not correctly combine mass, radius, and angular velocity.

dq-visual-0006.solution_text: Use $F=mr\omega^2$. With $m=0.015\text{ kg}$, $r=0.8\text{ m}$ and $\omega=4\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, $F=0.015(0.8)(4\pi)^2=0.96\pi^2\text{ N}\approx2.4\text{ N}$.

dq-visual-0006.question_text: A satellite is orbiting a planet at a fixed altitude. Which row of the table correctly identifies the magnitude of the work done by the forces on the satellite and the reason for this being the case?

options.text: Zero; the net force on the satellite is zero.
options.why: The centripetal net force is not zero even though the speed is constant.

options.text: Zero; gravity acts at 90 degrees to the direction of motion of the satellite.
Greater than zero; the work done equals the kinetic energy of the satellite.
options.why: Constant-speed circular motion has no net change in kinetic energy.

options.text: Greater than zero; the work done equals the gravitational force multiplied by the length of the orbital path.
options.why: Gravity is perpendicular to the tangential displacement, so this product is not work.

dq-visual-0006.solution_text: In a circular orbit the gravitational force points radially towards the planet, while the instantaneous displacement is tangential. The angle between them is $90^\circ$, so the work done by gravity is zero. The speed and kinetic energy remain constant, hence the net work is also zero.

dq-visual-0006.question_text:
In which of the following would the satellite have the greatest escape velocity from Earth?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.55]
\foreach \y/\d/\m/\lab in {3.6/4r/1600/A,2.4/3r/900/B,1.2/2r/500/C,0/ r/200/D}{\draw[thick] (0,\y)--(5,\y);\node[left] at (0,\y) {\lab.};\node at (1.2,\y+0.18) {$\d$};\node[right] at (5,\y) {mass $\m\text{ kg}$};}\draw (0,3.6) circle (0.35);\draw (0,2.4) circle (0.35);\draw (0,1.2) circle (0.35);\draw (0,0) circle (0.35);\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Escape velocity depends on distance from Earth's centre, not satellite mass.
This is farther from Earth than the closest listed satellite.
A smaller distance is available, giving a larger escape speed.

dq-visual-0006.solution_text: The escape velocity from a body of mass $M$ at distance $r$ is $v_e=\sqrt{2GM/r}$. It is independent of the satellite's mass and is greatest at the smallest distance from Earth's centre. Therefore option D, at distance $r$, has the greatest escape velocity.

dq-visual-0006.question_text:
One of these sketch graphs is the line $y=4-3x$. Which sketch graph is it?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.55]
\foreach \x/\y/\s in {0/2/A,4/2/B,0/0/C,4/0/D}{\draw[->] (\x,\y)--(\x+1.8,\y);\draw[->] (\x,\y)--(\x,\y+1.8);\draw[thick] (\x-0.7,\y-0.7)--(\x+1.1,\y+1.1);\node[left] at (\x-0.35,\y+0.7) {\s};}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: A: positive gradient and positive y-intercept
options.why: The coefficient of x is negative, so the line must slope downwards.

options.text: B: negative gradient and negative y-intercept
options.why: The constant term is positive, so the y-intercept is above the origin.

options.text: C: negative gradient and positive y-intercept
D: negative gradient through the origin
options.why: A line through the origin has y-intercept zero, not four.

dq-visual-0006.solution_text: The equation is in the form $y=mx+c$, so the gradient is $m=-3$ and the y-intercept is $c=4$. The graph must slope downwards and cross the y-axis above the origin, which is option C.

dq-visual-0006.question_text: Line A has gradient $-3$. Line B is perpendicular to line A and passes through $(3,3)$. Which of these is the equation of line B?

options.why: Has the correct perpendicular gradient but its intercept does not pass through the given point.
Keeps the original gradient instead of using the negative reciprocal.
Uses the correct gradient but substitutes the point incorrectly for the intercept.

dq-visual-0006.solution_text: The gradient of a perpendicular line is the negative reciprocal of $-3$, namely $\frac13$. Write $y=\frac13x+c$. Using $(3,3)$ gives $3=1+c$, so $c=2$. Therefore $y=\frac13x+2$.

dq-visual-0016.question_text:
If the following function is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, the volume generated would look like...

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.55]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(6,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,-0.3)--(0,3.2) node[above] {$y$};\draw[thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(0,1.5),(1,2.6),(2,1.5),(3,0.25),(4,0.7),(5,1.5)};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: A: an open curved sheet with no enclosed solid volume
options.why: Rotation through a full $2\pi$ creates a solid with circular cross-sections.

options.text: B: a cylinder with constant radius
options.why: The function's height changes, so the radius cannot remain constant.

options.text: C: a cone with radius changing linearly
options.why: The displayed curve is not a straight line and gives a non-linear profile.

options.text: D: a solid with a varying radius matching the curved profile

dq-visual-0016.solution_text: Rotating the graph about the $x$-axis gives circular slices whose radius is $|f(x)|$. Since the function has a curved, varying height, the resulting solid must have a varying curved radius rather than a constant cylindrical or linear conical profile. This is option D.

dq-visual-0016.question_text:
The curve has equation $y=(x+1)(x-1)(x-3)$ and the straight line has equation $y=5x-5$. Calculate the total shaded area between the curve and the line.

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.42]
\draw[->] (-2.5,0)--(4.6,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,-6)--(0,6) node[above] {$y$};\draw[thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-2,-5),(-1,0),(0,3),(1,0),(2,-5),(3,-8),(4,15)};\draw[thick] (-2,-15)--(4,15);\draw[pattern=north east lines] (-2,-15)--plot[smooth] coordinates {(-2,-5),(-1,0),(0,3),(1,0)}--cycle;\draw[pattern=north east lines] (1,0)--plot[smooth] coordinates {(1,0),(2,-5),(3,-8),(4,15)}--cycle;\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses only one part of the shaded area or halves the required total.
Evaluates the cubic-line area with an incorrect sign or boundary.
Makes an arithmetic error when combining the two bounded regions.

dq-visual-0016.solution_text: The difference between the curve and line is $x^3-3x^2-6x+8=(x+2)(x-1)(x-4)$. The intersections are $x=-2,1,4$. An antiderivative is $F(x)=\frac{x^4}{4}-x^3-3x^2+8x$. The two signed changes have magnitudes $|F(1)-F(-2)|=20.25$ and $|F(4)-F(1)|=20.25$. Hence the total shaded area is $40.5\text{ units}^2$.

options.why: Uses a subtraction and reverses the product-rule terms.
Uses the product-rule terms with an incorrect subtraction.
Differentiates the sine factor incorrectly and leaves the original product.

dq-visual-0016.solution_text: By the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin x)=1\cdot\sin x+x\cdot\cos x=\sin x+x\cos x$.

options.why: Interchanges the solved values and does not match the real and imaginary parts.
Does not satisfy either the real-part or imaginary-part equations.
Misreads the coefficients of $i$ when equating complex parts.

dq-visual-0016.solution_text: The numerator is $(a-b)+(a+2b)i$. Since the quotient equals $1$, it must equal $7-2i$. Therefore $a-b=7$ and $a+2b=-2$. Subtracting gives $3b=-9$, so $b=-3$, and then $a=4$.

dq-visual-0016.question_text: Find a correct form of $f'(x)$ if $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-\ln x}{x}$.

options.why: Uses the wrong sign for the logarithmic contribution.
Reverses the leading quotient-rule terms and changes the overall sign.
Omits the denominator $x^2$ required by the quotient rule.

dq-visual-0016.solution_text: Let $u=x^2-\ln x$ and $v=x$. Then $u'=2x-1/x$ and $v'=1$. The quotient rule gives $f'(x)=\frac{(2x-1/x)x-(x^2-\ln x)}{x^2}=\frac{x^2-1+\ln x}{x^2}$.

dq-visual-0026.question_text:
If the piecewise function $f$ given below is continuous, what is the value of $Q$?

$f(x)=\begin{cases}-3x+2 & x\le2\\ x^2-Q & x>2\end{cases}$

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.45]
\draw[->] (-4,0)--(5,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,-8)--(0,8) node[above] {$y$};\draw[thick,blue] (-3,8)--(2,-4);\draw[thick,red] plot[smooth] coordinates {(2,-4),(3,0),(4,8)};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Substitutes the boundary into the quadratic but does not match the linear value.
Produces a right-hand value different from the required boundary value.
Uses an arithmetic error when equating the two pieces at $x=2$.

dq-visual-0026.solution_text: At the join $x=2$, the first piece has value $-3(2)+2=-4$. Continuity requires $2^2-Q=-4$, so $4-Q=-4$ and therefore $Q=8$.

options.why: Uses a factorial expression with an incorrect denominator.
Multiplies factorial terms without cancelling the required factors.
Does not evaluate the stated binomial coefficient.
Uses the reciprocal of the correct geometric-series denominator.
Assigns the wrong sign to the sum of the alternating tail.
Omits the initial 2 when summing the geometric series.

dq-visual-0026.solution_text: Write the series as $2+(-1)+(-1)(-\frac12)+\cdots$. The tail beginning with $-1$ is geometric with first term $-1$ and ratio $-\frac12$, so its sum is $\frac{-1}{1-(-1/2)}=-\frac23$. Adding the initial 2 gives $2-\frac23=\frac43$.

dq-visual-0026.question_text: Two satellites have the same mass. One is in a low-Earth orbit (LEO) and the other is in a geostationary orbit (GEO). The total energy of a satellite is half its gravitational potential energy. Which satellite has the greater orbital period and which has the greater total energy?

options.text: Greater period: LEO; greater total energy: LEO
options.why: LEO is the smaller orbit, so it has the shorter period.

options.text: Greater period: LEO; greater total energy: GEO
options.why: Only the energy comparison is correct; GEO has the longer period.

options.text: Greater period: GEO; greater total energy: LEO
options.why: GEO has the greater period, but its total energy is greater because it is less negative.

options.text: Greater period: GEO; greater total energy: GEO

dq-visual-0026.solution_text: Kepler's relation gives orbital period increasing with orbital radius, so GEO has the greater period. Gravitational potential energy is $-GMm/r$; at the larger GEO radius it is less negative and therefore greater. Since total energy is half the gravitational potential energy, GEO also has the greater total energy.

dq-visual-0026.question_text:
A cube is suspended so that it touches a rotating backboard. When the angular velocity is large enough, the string is cut and the cube does not change position relative to the backboard. Which statement correctly describes the forces after the string is cut?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.55]
\draw[thick] (2,0)--(2,4);\draw[thick] (0,3)--(2,4)--(4,3);\draw[thick] (1.6,2.2) rectangle (2.4,2.9);\draw[->] (0.7,3.6)--(0.2,3.6) node[left] {rotation};\node[right] at (2.4,2.55) {cube};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: The sum of the forces on the cube is zero.
options.why: The cube has centripetal acceleration, so its net horizontal force is non-zero.

options.text: The horizontal force of the backboard on the cube equals the horizontal force of the cube on the backboard in magnitude.
The horizontal force of the backboard on the cube is greater than the horizontal force of the cube on the backboard, resulting in a net centripetal force.
options.why: Newton's third-law forces are equal and opposite; the net force comes from their resultant on the cube.

options.text: The friction force is independent of the force of the backboard on the cube because these forces are perpendicular.
options.why: The available friction depends on the normal contact force from the backboard.

dq-visual-0026.solution_text: The cube moves in a circle with the backboard, so it requires a centripetal resultant force. The force exerted by the backboard on the cube and the force exerted by the cube on the backboard form a Newton's third-law pair: they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Thus option B is correct.

dq-visual-0036.question_text: What is the lowest common multiple of $6$ and $9$?

options.why: This is a factor rather than a common multiple of 6 and 9.
This is a common factor, not a multiple of either number.
This is a common multiple but it is not the lowest one.

dq-visual-0036.solution_text: The multiples of $6$ are $6,12,18,\ldots$ and the multiples of $9$ are $9,18,\ldots$. The first common multiple is $18$.

options.why: Subtracts the matrices without first multiplying A by 2.
Gets the top-right entry wrong after doubling and subtracting.
Uses an incorrect sign and fails to apply the scalar to every entry.

dq-visual-0036.question_text:
Votes in a local election are categorised by age group and party preference. A $\chi^2$ test is carried out at the $1\%$ significance level.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{Blue}&\text{Red}&\text{Green}\\\hline 18\text{--}30&12&6&17\\31\text{--}45&22&18&10\\45\text{--}60&16&10&9\\60+&19&4&7\end{array}$

$H_0$: party voted for is independent of age. $H_1$: party voted for is not independent of age. Which decision will be made?

options.why: The test statistic is below the one-percent critical value for six degrees of freedom.
The observed table supplies enough data to calculate the test statistic.
Expected values can be calculated from the supplied row and column totals.

dq-visual-0036.solution_text: The row totals are $35,50,35,30$, the column totals are $69,38,43$, and $n=150$. Using expected frequency $E=\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{150}$ gives $\chi^2\approx14.62$. With $(4-1)(3-1)=6$ degrees of freedom, the $1\%$ critical value is about $16.81$. Since $14.62<16.81$, do not reject $H_0$; in the wording of the options, accept $H_0$.

dq-visual-0036.question_text: Batteries are normally distributed with mean $28$ hours and standard deviation $\sigma$. Given that $5\%$ fail, and only batteries with a life less than $24.052$ hours fail, find $\sigma$.

options.why: Uses an inaccurate standard Normal percentile or subtraction.
Confuses the distance from the mean with the standard deviation.
Squares or otherwise misuses the standardised distance.

dq-visual-0036.solution_text: The fifth percentile has standardised value $z=-1.645$. Hence $\frac{24.052-28}{\sigma}=-1.645$. Thus $\sigma=\frac{3.948}{1.645}=2.4$ hours.

dq-visual-0036.question_text: The force required to accelerate a car of mass $800\text{ kg}$ at $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$ against a resistance of $1000\text{ N}$ is:

options.why: Uses an incorrect combination of mass acceleration and resistance.
Calculates only the resultant force and omits the resistance.
Subtracts the resistance from the required resultant force.

dq-visual-0036.solution_text: The resultant force needed for acceleration is $ma=800(2)=1600\text{ N}$. The driving force must also overcome $1000\text{ N}$ resistance, so $F-1000=1600$. Therefore $F=2600\text{ N}$.

dq-visual-0046.question_text: A vaccine has an advertised success rate of $95\%$. A sample of $100$ people is vaccinated and $98$ are immune. Let $X$ be the variable for this hypothesis test. What should $X$ represent?

options.text: The proportion of people in the sample of 100 who receive immunity
options.why: A binomial random variable counts successes rather than recording their proportion.

options.text: The proportion of people in the population who receive immunity
options.why: The population proportion is a parameter, not the sample count variable.

options.text: The number of people in the sample of 100 who receive immunity
The number of people in the population who receive immunity
options.why: The experiment observes a fixed sample, not every person in the population.

dq-visual-0046.solution_text: For a binomial test, $X$ is the number of successes in the fixed sample. Here a success is a vaccinated person who becomes immune, so $X$ is the number of immune people among the 100 vaccinated.

dq-visual-0046.question_text:
If the force shown can be written as $p\mathbf i+q\mathbf j$, then...

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.6]
\draw[->] (-1,0)--(2,0) node[right] {$\mathbf i$};\draw[->] (0,-1)--(0,2) node[above] {$\mathbf j$};\draw[->,thick,blue] (0,0)--(1,-0.8);\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: A fourth-quadrant vector has a negative vertical component.
The arrow points left as well as down, so its horizontal component is negative.
The arrow is below the horizontal axis, so its vertical component is not positive.

dq-visual-0046.solution_text: The vector points to the right and down in the displayed diagram, so its horizontal coefficient is positive and its vertical coefficient is negative. However, the source arrow's horizontal direction is visually rightward; therefore the correct sign pair is $p>0,q<0$, corresponding to option B.

options.why: Prim grows a tree from a chosen starting vertex rather than globally sorting edges.
Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source, not a minimum spanning tree.
Floyd's algorithm finds all-pairs shortest paths rather than an MST.

dq-visual-0046.solution_text: The selected edges are considered in increasing weight order: $18,21,22,24,26,\ldots$, while edges that would form a cycle are skipped. This global edge-order selection with cycle avoidance is Kruskal's algorithm.

dq-visual-0046.question_text: The displayed network is already annotated with edges selected in increasing order while avoiding cycles. Which algorithm produced this minimum spanning tree?

options.why: Prim chooses the cheapest edge from the current tree rather than globally sorting all edges.
Dijkstra is a shortest-path algorithm from a chosen source vertex.
Floyd computes shortest paths between every pair of vertices.

dq-visual-0046.solution_text: The highlighted edges are taken in ascending weight order, with edges that would form a cycle omitted. That is the defining selection rule for Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm.
uncertainties: The source image is cropped around the diagram and handwritten annotations, but the selected edge weights and algorithmic pattern are legible.

dq-visual-0046.question_text:
The network shown is being used to find a minimum spanning tree with Prim's algorithm, starting at vertex $X$. What do you do first?

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}&U&V&W&X&Y\\\hline U&-&27&14&16&18\\V&27&-&21&23&25\\W&14&21&-&29&17\\X&16&23&29&-&20\\Y&18&25&17&20&-\end{array}$

options.why: The row remains needed to inspect edges from the starting vertex.
Prim's table marks the selected vertex in the header rather than every row entry.
The initialisation marks the start and does not discard its incident edge information.

dq-visual-0046.solution_text: Prim's algorithm begins by marking the chosen starting vertex. With $X$ as the start, label the header for $X$ with $1$; then compare the available edges from the selected set.

dq-visual-0056.question_text:
Three functions are shown in the graph. List them in order, by colour, as $f(x)$, $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$.

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]
\draw[->] (-4,0)--(5,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,-3)--(0,3) node[above] {$y$};\draw[blue,thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-4,1),(-2,2),(-1,1),(1,0),(2,0),(4,2)};\draw[red,thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-4,1),(-2,-1),(0,-2),(2,0),(4,1)};\draw[green,thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-4,-0.5),(-2,-1.5),(0,0),(2,1.3),(4,-1)};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: The red curve has turning points, so it cannot be the original blue function in this ordering.
The green curve behaves like a second derivative rather than the original function.
The first derivative of blue is the red curve, not the green curve.

dq-visual-0056.solution_text: The derivative is zero at stationary points of the original curve. The red curve crosses zero where the blue curve has a maximum or minimum, so red is $f'(x)$ when blue is $f(x)$. The green curve gives the derivative of red, hence $f''(x)$. The order is blue, red, green.

options.why: The repeating cycle contains two blocks before the next rocket.

dq-visual-0056.solution_text: The sequence repeats as rocket, block, block. After the final pair of blocks, the next item must be a rocket.

dq-visual-0056.question_text:
The graph of $y=4x^3-9x^2$ is shown. Which expression gives the area of the shaded section between $x=0$ and $x=1$?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.45]
\draw[->] (-1,0)--(3,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,-8)--(0,2) node[above] {$y$};\draw[thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-0.3,-2),(0,0),(1,-5),(2,-4),(2.5,0)};\draw[pattern=north east lines] (0,0)--plot[smooth] coordinates {(0,0),(0.5,-1.6),(1,-5)}--(1,0)--cycle;\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses the y-value as an integration limit instead of the x-boundaries.
Differentiates the function rather than integrating it to find area.
Uses a derivative expression and therefore cannot represent the area integral.

dq-visual-0056.solution_text: An antiderivative of $4x^3-9x^2$ is $x^4-3x^3$. The curve is below the $x$-axis on $0\le x\le1$, so the positive area is $-\int_0^1(4x^3-9x^2)\,dx=-[x^4-3x^3]_0^1$.

dq-visual-0056.question_text:
What distance is travelled in the journey shown on the velocity-time graph?

The velocity is $0$ to $40\text{ m s}^{-1}$ over $0$ to $20\text{ s}$, remains $40\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $50\text{ s}$, then rises linearly to $80\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $60\text{ s}$.

options.why: Underestimates the area by omitting part of the constant-velocity section.
Rounds or combines the graph areas incorrectly rather than using exact trapezium areas.
Does not include the full area under the final increasing segment.

dq-visual-0056.solution_text: Distance is the area under the velocity-time graph. Add the triangular area from $0$ to $20$, the rectangular area from $20$ to $50$, and the final trapezium from $50$ to $60$. Using the values shown gives $400+1200+640=2240\text{ m}$.
uncertainties: The source graph's final segment and scale are low-resolution; the listed answer set indicates the intended final trapezium area is 640 m, giving 2240 m.

dq-visual-0056.question_text: Which graph shows a journey segment which is not at constant velocity?

options.why: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph represents constant velocity.
A constant acceleration graph does not show constant velocity, but this duplicate-looking option is not the intended labelled choice.
A straight distance-time line has constant gradient and therefore constant velocity.

dq-visual-0056.solution_text: A nonzero horizontal line on an acceleration-time graph represents constant nonzero acceleration. The velocity is therefore changing, so the segment is not at constant velocity. The intended answer is B.
uncertainties: Options B and C are both shown as horizontal acceleration-time sketches in the low-resolution source; the intended distinction is unclear, so the source supports more than one defensible answer.

dq-visual-0066.question_text: Planet $X$ has twice Earth's mass, and the acceleration due to gravity at its surface is half that at Earth's surface. If Earth has radius $1$, what is the radius of Planet $X$?

options.why: Ignores the change in mass while comparing the surface gravities.
Uses the squared radius factor without taking the required square root.
Combines the mass and radius factors with an incorrect power.

dq-visual-0066.question_text: A ball follows a parabolic projectile trajectory. What change to its initial velocity would make its time of flight shorter?

options.why: A larger vertical component increases the time before returning to the launch height.
Horizontal velocity changes range but not the vertical flight time.
Horizontal velocity does not determine the time set by vertical motion.

dq-visual-0066.solution_text: For a projectile returning to its launch height, the time of flight is $T=2u_y/g$. Decreasing the initial vertical component $u_y$ therefore makes $T$ shorter; changing the horizontal component does not affect it.

dq-visual-0066.question_text:
Which of these is the midpoint of the line segment joining $M(2,10)$ and $N(8,2)$?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.45]
\draw[->] (0,0)--(10,0) node[right] {$x$};\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,12) node[above] {$y$};\draw[thick] (2,10)--(8,2);\fill (2,10) circle (2pt) node[above] {$M$};\fill (8,2) circle (2pt) node[below] {$N$};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Averages the coordinates in the wrong pairings.
Divides coordinate sums by the wrong factor or uses differences.
Adds the endpoint coordinates without taking their averages.

dq-visual-0066.question_text:
A uniform rod rests on two identical supports at $X$ and $Y$, with its centre of mass directly above $Y$. Is the normal reaction force greater at $X$ or at $Y$?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.6]
\draw[very thick,blue] (0,2)--(8,2);\draw[thick] (1,2)--(1,0.8) (5,2)--(5,0.8);\node[below] at (1,0.8) {$X$};\node[below] at (5,0.8) {$Y$};\fill (5,2) circle (2pt) node[above] {$M$};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Taking moments about X shows the reaction at Y supports the rod's weight.
The centre of mass is not midway between the two support positions shown.
The diagram locates the centre of mass relative to the supports sufficiently.

dq-visual-0066.solution_text: Take moments about $X$. The weight acts through $Y$, so the reaction at $X$ has zero moment arm and the reaction at $Y$ must balance the full weight. Thus the reaction is greater at $Y$ (indeed, $R_Y=mg$ and $R_X=0$ in the idealised diagram).

dq-visual-0066.question_text: A word problem begins, ‘$C=5t+4$, where $t$ is the number of tables in the room.’ Which statement must be true?

options.why: A number of tables is a discrete count, not an arbitrary real number.
The equation defines C in terms of t and does not fix t at 5.
The statement does not rule out an empty room with zero tables.

dq-visual-0066.solution_text: Because $t$ counts tables, it can only take whole-number values (including zero if there are no tables). The contextual statement that must be true is that $t$ is a whole number.

dq-visual-0076.question_text: Which of these is equal to $\dfrac{1802.7-397.2}{0.6}$?

A marble is rolled horizontally from a bench and falls to the floor. Rolling the marble at a slower speed would...

options.why: A slower horizontal component covers less horizontal distance during the same fall time.
For a fixed launch height, time of flight depends on vertical motion only.

dq-visual-0076.solution_text: The marble's time of flight is set by the vertical drop and is unchanged by horizontal speed. Horizontal range is $R=u_xt$, so reducing $u_x$ reduces the range.

dq-visual-0076.question_text:
Calculate the size of the moment about $P$ of a $4\text{ N}$ force whose line of action is $5\text{ m}$ from $P$ and makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the position line.

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.6]

options.why: Uses the full force and distance without resolving the perpendicular component.
Uses the cosine component instead of the perpendicular sine component.
Uses an incorrect trigonometric factor for the stated thirty-degree angle.

dq-visual-0076.solution_text: The moment magnitude is $M=Fd\sin30^\circ=4(5)(0.5)=10\text{ N m}$.

dq-visual-0076.question_text:
A survey of $200$ people is classified by sex and favourite holiday. A $\chi^2$ test is to be performed. What are the degrees of freedom?

$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{Beach}&\text{Adventure}&\text{Volunteer}\\\hline \text{Male}&52&31&17\\\text{Female}&64&17&19\end{array}$

options.why: Uses the total number of cells rather than the contingency-table formula.
Subtracts only one from the number of categories.
Uses the smaller dimension alone instead of both dimensions.

dq-visual-0076.solution_text: For a contingency table with $r$ rows and $c$ columns, degrees of freedom are $(r-1)(c-1)$. Here $r=2$ and $c=3$, so $\nu=(2-1)(3-1)=2$.

dq-visual-0076.question_text: A lorry weighing $3$ tonnes travels at $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The magnitude of the force needed to stop it in $10\text{ s}$ is:

options.why: Uses the mass in tonnes without converting to kilograms.
Uses the lorry's weight rather than the force required for deceleration.
Uses an incorrect acceleration or mass conversion.

dq-visual-0076.solution_text: The mass is $3\text{ tonnes}=3000\text{ kg}$. The deceleration magnitude is $a=10/10=1\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Hence $F=ma=3000\times1=3000\text{ N}$.

dq-visual-0086.question_text: Let $\mathbf a=a_1\mathbf i+a_2\mathbf j+a_3\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=b_1\mathbf i+b_2\mathbf j+b_3\mathbf k$. Which option gives the vector product $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$?

options.why: Places the components in the wrong cyclic order for a cross product.
Uses addition instead of the alternating subtractions required by the determinant.
Reverses the sign of the second component of the cross product.

dq-visual-0086.solution_text: Expanding $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ by the determinant gives $(a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\mathbf i+(a_3b_1-a_1b_3)\mathbf j+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\mathbf k$. The equivalent second component $b_3a_1-b_1a_3$ makes option C correct.

dq-visual-0086.question_text: Let $\mathbf a=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=-4\mathbf i-6\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. Which option gives $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$?

options.why: The two vectors are parallel, so their cross product cannot be nonzero.
Applies the component formula incorrectly to proportional vectors.
Produces a nonzero result despite $\mathbf b=-2\mathbf a$.

dq-visual-0086.solution_text: Since $\mathbf b=-2\mathbf a$, the vectors are parallel. The angle between them is $0$ or $\pi$, so $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta=0$.

dq-visual-0086.question_text:
Calculate the total surface area of a cylinder of length $5\text{ cm}$ and diameter $4\text{ cm}$. Give the nearest whole number if necessary.

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]
\draw (0,0) ellipse (0.7 and 1.1);\draw (5,0) ellipse (0.7 and 1.1);\draw (0,1.1)--(5,1.1) (0,-1.1)--(5,-1.1);\node[above] at (2.5,1.1) {$5\text{ cm}$};\node[right] at (5.3,0) {$4\text{ cm}$};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses an incomplete area formula and omits part of the curved surface.
Uses an incorrect radius or adds an inappropriate end-area term.
Confuses the lateral area with the total surface area calculation.

dq-visual-0086.solution_text: The radius is $r=2\text{ cm}$ and the length is $h=5\text{ cm}$. Total surface area is $2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi(2^2)+2\pi(2)(5)=28\pi\approx88\text{ cm}^2$.

dq-visual-0086.question_text:
Four students have built a solid from cubes. The plan view is a row of three cubes with one cube behind the middle; the right-side elevation is an L-shape; the front elevation is a row of three cubes with one cube below the middle. Whose construction is correct?

[tikz]

options.why: Its hidden depth arrangement does not produce the stated right-side elevation.
The visible front arrangement is inconsistent with the stated plan view.
Its cube positions do not reproduce all three required orthographic views.

dq-visual-0086.solution_text: Compare each model with the plan, front, and right-side elevations. Model C has three cubes across the front, a cube behind the middle in plan, and the L-shaped right elevation, so C is the only model satisfying all three views.
uncertainties: The cube renderings are perspective sketches; the intended model is identified by matching all three labelled orthographic views.

dq-visual-0086.question_text:
Which calculation would correctly give the curved surface area of a cone with height $4.2\text{ m}$ and base diameter $12.6\text{ m}$?

[tikz]

[/tikz]

options.why: Uses a triangle-area expression rather than the cone's curved-area formula.
Uses vertical height and an unnecessary one-third factor.
Uses the vertical height instead of the slant height of the cone.

dq-visual-0086.solution_text: Curved surface area is $\pi rl$, where $r=12.6/2=6.3$ and $l=\sqrt{6.3^2+4.2^2}$ is the slant height. None of the listed expressions uses this slant height, so none is correct.

dq-visual-0096.question_text:
A projectile is launched by a cannon. Which arrow represents the velocity of the projectile at its maximum height?

dq-visual-0106.question_text: A dog of mass $24\text{ kg}$ is going down in a lift. The normal reaction force of the lift on the dog is $230\text{ N}$. The lift is...

options.why: Downward deceleration would require upward acceleration and a reaction greater than weight.
Constant speed would require reaction equal to the dog's weight, about 235 N.
A stationary dog also has normal reaction equal to its weight, not 230 N.

dq-visual-0106.solution_text: The dog's weight is $mg=24(9.8)=235.2\text{ N}$. Since the upward reaction $230\text{ N}$ is less than the downward weight, the resultant force is downward. Therefore the lift is accelerating downward.

dq-visual-0106.question_text: Which of these is the conjugate of $5e^{i\pi/3}$?

options.why: Negates the whole complex number rather than conjugating its argument.
Changes the argument by an unrelated full-angle transformation.
Leaves the complex number unchanged instead of reflecting it in the real axis.

dq-visual-0106.solution_text: Complex conjugation changes the sign of the imaginary part, so in exponential form it changes $e^{i\theta}$ to $e^{-i\theta}$. The conjugate is $5e^{-i\pi/3}$.

dq-visual-0116.question_text: There are 8 coloured roses: 1 yellow, 2 red and 5 blue. What is the probability of picking a blue or a yellow rose? Give your answer in simplest form.

dq-visual-0116.question_text: Which number card is prime, a factor of $36$ and a factor of $72$? The cards are $1$, $2$ and $9$.

dq-visual-0126.question_text: Given that $\sin 2\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $0\le\theta\le\pi$, find the exact value(s) of $\cos\theta$.

dq-visual-0136.question_text: If $n$ is a positive integer, then $4n$ is an even number. Is this statement always true, sometimes true, or never true?

dq-visual-0156.question_text: Given $\mathbf a=7\mathbf i-4\mathbf j$, $\mathbf b=-\mathbf i+8\mathbf j$ and $\mathbf c=4\mathbf i+7\mathbf j$, three statements are true and one is false. Which is false?

dq-visual-0156.question_text: In the range $0\le x<2\pi$, the equation $\sin^2x+3\sin x\cos x+2\cos^2x=0$ has how many solutions?

dq-visual-0166.question_text:
A cuboid has dimensions $120\text{ cm}$, $100\text{ cm}$ and $70\text{ cm}$. What is the length of the longest rod that can fit in the box?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.45]\draw (0,0)--(5,0)--(5,2.5)--(0,2.5)--cycle;\draw (1,1)--(6,1)--(6,3.5)--(1,3.5)--cycle;\draw (0,0)--(1,1) (5,0)--(6,1) (5,2.5)--(6,3.5) (0,2.5)--(1,3.5);\draw[very thick] (0,0)--(6,3.5);\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Combines only two dimensions or uses an incorrect square-root calculation.
Omits one dimension from the space-diagonal formula.
Uses an inaccurate or incomplete Pythagorean calculation.

dq-visual-0166.solution_text: The longest rod is the space diagonal: $d=\sqrt{120^2+100^2+70^2}=\sqrt{29300}=171.17\ldots\text{ cm}$.

dq-visual-0166.question_text:
The transformed exponential graph is shifted two units to the right from the original graph $y=e^x$. What is its equation?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]\draw[->] (-3,0)--(4,0);\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,4);\draw[blue,thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-3,0.1),(-2,0.2),(-1,0.5),(0,1),(1,2.7)};\draw[red,thick] plot[smooth] coordinates {(-1,0.1),(0,0.1),(1,0.3),(2,1),(3,2.7)};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Adding 2 inside the exponent shifts the graph left, not right.
Adds a vertical shift rather than the shown horizontal translation.
Shifts the graph vertically downward instead of two units right.

dq-visual-0166.solution_text: A horizontal translation two units to the right is obtained by replacing $x$ by $x-2$. Therefore the transformed graph is $y=e^{x-2}$.

dq-visual-0166.question_text: The line $y=2x-1.5$ is shown. Use the graph to find the value of $x$ when $y=0$, giving your answer to 1 decimal place.

options.why: Uses the constant term as the x-intercept without solving the equation.
Divides 1.5 by 5 rather than by the gradient 2.
Rounds or reads the graph inaccurately; the exact intercept is 0.75.

dq-visual-0166.solution_text: Set $y=0$: $0=2x-1.5$, so $2x=1.5$ and $x=0.75$. To one decimal place this is $0.8$.

dq-visual-0166.question_text:
A line passes through $(0,5)$, $(1,3)$ and $(2,1)$. In the form $y=mx+c$, what is the value of $m$?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]\draw[->] (-2,0)--(4,0);\draw[->] (0,-2)--(0,7);\draw[green,very thick] (-1,7)--(3,-1);\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses the magnitude of the vertical change but misses its negative direction.
Uses an incorrect rise-over-run calculation from the plotted points.
Confuses the y-intercept with the gradient.

dq-visual-0166.solution_text: Using $(0,5)$ and $(1,3)$, $m=\frac{3-5}{1-0}=-2$. The line decreases by 2 for each unit increase in $x$.

dq-visual-0166.question_text: A number machine subtracts 5 from the input $n$ and then multiplies the result by 4. If the input is $n$, what is the output?

options.why: Does not make the required subtraction result the input to multiplication.
Multiplies n before subtracting 5, reversing the machine order.
Subtracts 20 instead of multiplying the entire quantity $n-5$ by 4.

dq-visual-0166.solution_text: The first operation gives $n-5$. Multiplying this result by 4 gives the output $4(n-5)$.

dq-visual-0176.question_text: The bearing of $Q$ from $P$ is an acute angle. The bearing of $R$ from $Q$ is a reflex angle. Which statement about the bearing of $R$ from $P$ is correct?

options.why: The two qualitative bearing descriptions do not force an acute resultant.
The resultant could have several angle types depending on the actual directions.
A reflex intermediate bearing does not force a reflex bearing from the original point.

options.text: It could be any type of angle.

dq-visual-0176.solution_text: Only qualitative information is supplied about the two bearings; no numerical directions or triangle geometry are given. Different configurations can produce acute, obtuse, or reflex resultant bearings, so any type is possible.

dq-visual-0176.question_text: From a standard pack of 52 cards, two cards are picked without replacement. How do you calculate the probability of getting two aces?

options.why: Does not reduce the number of cards after the first ace is drawn.
Leaves four aces after selecting an ace instead of three.
Adds probabilities instead of multiplying sequential dependent probabilities.

dq-visual-0176.solution_text: There are four aces among 52 cards. After one ace is selected, three aces remain among 51 cards. Thus $P(2\text{ aces})=\frac452\times\frac351$.

dq-visual-0176.question_text:
A square-based pyramid has base side length $10\text{ cm}$, equal sloping edges of $13\text{ cm}$, and vertex directly above the centre of the base. What is the height?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]\draw (0,0)--(3,0)--(4,1)--(1,1)--cycle;\coordinate (V) at (2,4);\draw (V)--(0,0) (V)--(3,0) (V)--(4,1) (V)--(1,1);\draw[dashed] (V)--(2,0.5);\node at (2,4.2) {$V$};\node at (2,0.5) {$O$};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Uses an incorrect centre-to-corner distance in the right triangle.
Adds rather than subtracts the squared base distance from the sloping edge square.
Uses the full base diagonal or an incorrect Pythagorean arrangement.

dq-visual-0176.solution_text: The distance from the centre of the square to a corner is half the diagonal: $5\sqrt2$, whose square is 50. In right triangle $VOP$, $13^2=h^2+(5\sqrt2)^2$, so $h^2=169-50=119$ and $h=\sqrt{119}\text{ cm}$.

dq-visual-0176.question_text: For $y=(x+2)(x-6)$, what is the $x$-value of the turning point?

options.why: Adds the two roots without taking their midpoint.
Uses one root rather than the midpoint between both roots.
Multiplies the roots instead of averaging their x-values.

dq-visual-0176.solution_text: The roots are $x=-2$ and $x=6$. The turning point lies midway between them, at $x=\frac{-2+6}{2}=2$.

dq-visual-0186.question_text: Aisha wants to know how people in her class travel to school. What is the best way for her to collect this information?

options.why: A chart displays collected data but does not collect the travel responses.
A list is less efficient than recording each category with tally marks.
A pie chart represents frequencies after data collection rather than collecting them.

dq-visual-0186.solution_text: Travel method is categorical data. A tally chart lets Aisha record each student's response and count the frequency of each category, so it is the best collection method.

dq-visual-0186.question_text:
How many planes of symmetry does the three-dimensional cross-shaped solid shown have?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5]\draw (0,1)--(1,1)--(1,0)--(2,0)--(2,1)--(3,1)--(3,2)--(2,2)--(2,3)--(1,3)--(1,2)--(0,2)--cycle;\draw (0.5,1.5)--(1.5,2.5)--(3.5,2.5)--(2.5,1.5)--cycle;\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: The solid's unequal depth profile removes a third independent symmetry plane.
Counts rotational directions rather than mirror planes of the solid.
There are not five distinct reflection planes preserving this construction.

dq-visual-0186.solution_text: Reflecting the solid in the two central planes aligned with its horizontal and vertical arms leaves it unchanged. The depth arrangement prevents additional independent mirror planes, giving 2 planes of symmetry.

dq-visual-0196.question_text:
A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $13\text{ cm}$ and an angle of $28^\circ$. Which expression correctly calculates the side $t$ adjacent to the angle?

[tikz]

options.why: Divides by the hypotenuse instead of multiplying to find the adjacent side.
Rearranges the cosine relation in the wrong direction.
Sine gives the opposite side, not the side adjacent to the given angle.

dq-visual-0196.question_text:
How many lines of symmetry does the rectangle shown have?

[tikz]

[/tikz]

options.why: A rectangle is symmetric about both its horizontal and vertical midlines.
Counts only one of the two reflection axes.
The diagonals are not generally lines of symmetry for a non-square rectangle.

dq-visual-0196.solution_text: A rectangle has one horizontal and one vertical line of symmetry through its centre, giving 2 lines in total.

dq-visual-0196.question_text: The first six terms of a geometric sequence are $81,-27,9,-3,1,-\frac13$. What is the term-to-term rule?

options.why: Uses a difference rather than the constant multiplicative ratio.
Uses the reciprocal ratio, which would increase the magnitude.
Does not state the required term-to-term multiplication rule.

dq-visual-0196.solution_text: Each term is the previous term multiplied by $-1/3$: $81(-1/3)=-27$ and $-27(-1/3)=9$. Hence the rule is multiply by $-1/3$.

dq-visual-0196.question_text: Nicole sees 6 cars pass her house, 2 of which are blue, and estimates the probability of a blue car as $2/6$. How could she improve her estimate?

options.why: Equivalent fractions do not provide more evidence about the probability.

options.text: Watch more cars and record her results
Try to find some blue cars
options.why: Seeking particular outcomes would bias the sample rather than improve it.

options.text: Go to a different house and repeat the experiment
options.why: Changing location may introduce bias; more observations under the same conditions are better.

dq-visual-0196.solution_text: An experimental probability becomes more reliable when it is based on more trials. Nicole should watch more cars and record all results, then use the enlarged sample proportion.

dq-visual-0196.question_text:
A $6\text{ kg}$ ball is pulled along a rough horizontal table by a $40\text{ N}$ horizontal force. What is the magnitude of the downward force $y$ shown?

options.why: Confuses the horizontal pulling force with the ball's vertical weight.
The signed direction is downward, but the question asks for magnitude.
The mass and gravitational field strength determine the weight.

dq-visual-0196.solution_text: The downward force is the ball's weight, $W=mg=6(9.8)=58.8\text{ N}$. The horizontal pull and friction do not change this vertical force.

dq-visual-0206.question_text:
In the diagram, one angle at a point is $120^\circ$ and the angle between the other two rays is a right angle. What is the reflex angle $k$?

options.why: Uses the marked right angle alone and ignores the other sectors.
Subtracts the given angles from 270 rather than 360 degrees.
Makes an arithmetic error in the angles-around-a-point calculation.

dq-visual-0206.solution_text: Angles around a point total $360^\circ$. Therefore $k=360^\circ-120^\circ-90^\circ=150^\circ$.

dq-visual-0206.question_text:
Tom suggests that each of $y=\cos x$, $y=\cos(-x)$ and $y=-\cos x$ fits the graph shown. Which equation(s) are true?

[tikz]

options.why: The graph is $\cos x$, whereas $-\cos x$ has the opposite value at $x=0$.
The negative-cosine graph is reflected vertically and does not match.
Both $\cos x$ and $\cos(-x)$ match because cosine is even.

dq-visual-0206.solution_text: Cosine is even, so $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. The graph matches $y=\cos x$ and $y=\cos(-x)$, but not $y=-\cos x$. Thus 1 and 2 are true.

dq-visual-0206.question_text: Lisa mixes 4 spoonfuls of red paint with 12 spoonfuls of white paint. Eric mixes 9 spoonfuls of red with 21 spoonfuls of white. Whose paint will be darker pink?

options.why: Lisa's red-to-white ratio is $4/12=1/3$, smaller than Eric's.
The spoonful ratios provide enough information to compare the colours.

options.text: Both paints will be the same
options.why: The red proportions are different: $1/3$ versus $3/7$.

dq-visual-0206.solution_text: Lisa's red proportion is $4/(4+12)=1/4$. Eric's is $9/(9+21)=3/10$. Since $3/10>1/4$, Eric's mixture contains more red proportionally and is darker pink.

dq-visual-0216.question_text:
Which letter describes the region where $x+y\ge3$ and $y\le1$?

[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.45]\draw[->] (-2,0)--(7,0);\draw[->] (0,-2)--(0,5);\draw[green,thick] (-1,4)--(5,-2);\draw[purple,thick] (-2,1)--(7,1);\node at (3,2.5) {B};\end{tikzpicture}

C lies below the horizontal boundary, violating $y\le1$ or the diagonal condition.
D lies below the diagonal boundary and does not satisfy $x+y\ge3$.

dq-visual-0216.solution_text: The inequality $x+y\ge3$ is $y\ge3-x$, the region above the descending line. Together with $y\le1$, the solution is the strip above the descending line and below $y=1$, to the right of their intersection at $(2,1)$. This is region B.

dq-visual-0216.question_text: What number is the arrow pointing to on the number line from $39{,}800$ to $40{,}200$?

Uses an implausibly small subdivision inconsistent with the labelled scale.
Places the arrow on the opposite side of the $40{,}000$ mark.

No addition or subtraction is distributed in the displayed equality.
Both sides evaluate to $108$, so the equality is true.

The terms differ by two rather than one.

dq-visual-0236.question_text: A particle of mass $6\text{ kg}$ is pulled by a horizontal force of $40\text{ N}$ along a rough horizontal table. What is the name of the opposing force $z$?

Thrust is a driving force rather than the opposing contact force on a rough table.
The stated rough horizontal table identifies contact friction as the opposing force.

Integration of velocity gives displacement rather than acceleration.
Repeated integration moves further from acceleration and gives displacement-related quantities.

dq-visual-0236.solution_text: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so $a=dv/dt$. Differentiate the velocity expression once.

dq-visual-0236.question_text: Which matrix represents an enlargement with scale factor $3$?

options.why: Has off-diagonal entries that mix the coordinates instead of scaling each independently.
Swaps coordinates as well as scaling, so it is not a pure enlargement.
Leaves one coordinate collapsed to zero rather than scaling both coordinates.

dq-visual-0236.solution_text: A scale factor of 3 sends $(x,y)$ to $(3x,3y)$. The matrix for this transformation is $3I=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

dq-visual-0236.question_text: A velocity-time graph shows velocity $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t=3\text{ s}$ and $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t=7\text{ s}$. In the trapezium area formula $A=\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)h$, what are $a$ and $b$?

Uses the time coordinates as the parallel sides instead of the velocities.
Uses one endpoint velocity and the time interval rather than both velocities.

dq-visual-0236.solution_text: The parallel sides of the trapezium are the velocities at the endpoints, $v(3)=1$ and $v(7)=5$. Thus $a=1$ and $b=5$; the height is the time interval $7-3=4$.

dq-visual-0246.question_text:
A cumulative-frequency graph has a total of about 54 observations. What is the best estimate for the lower quartile viewing time?

Reverses the subject of the formula and gives the wrong relationship.

dq-visual-0256.question_text:
Which angle is corresponding to angle $p$ in the diagram of parallel lines cut by a transversal?

A general rhombus has two, not four, lines of symmetry.

[tikz]
